title: Health policy, legislation and economics
blurb: Explain devolved UK differences, QALYs, cost-effectiveness and opportunity cost, current policy changes, and how nurses influence policy.
question: A new treatment costs £30,000 more than current care and gives an extra 1.5 quality-adjusted life years. How does its cost per QALY compare with NICE's standard threshold from 2026?

teach.h: Policy, law and money shape care
teach.body: Health legislation (Acts of Parliament and regulations) and policy (government and NHS decisions) decide how services are organised, regulated and funded. Health is devolved, so England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each run their own health systems and some laws differ. Health economics asks how to get the most health from limited resources. In plain English: the rules, the structures and the budget all affect what care a nurse can give (proficiencies P7.2–P7.4).

head: Nation
Health and care regulator
Capacity law
teach.caption: The NMC regulates nurses and midwives UK-wide; nursing associates are regulated in England only.

teach.body: Every health budget is limited, so choosing to fund one thing means something else is not funded. NICE defines opportunity cost as the value of the benefits from other healthcare programmes displaced by an intervention, best measured by the health that could have been gained by spending the money on the next best alternative. This is why cost-effectiveness matters: a treatment that costs a lot for little benefit can take health away from others.
teach.cite: NICE glossary: opportunity costs; proficiency P7.3

teach.h: QALYs: weighting each year by quality of life
teach.caption: QALYs = years of life × quality-of-life score (0 to 1). Two years at 0.5 = 1 QALY (NICE glossary).
NICE's standard threshold for technology appraisals rose from £20,000–£30,000 to £25,000–£35,000 per QALY gained (2026). Cost is not the only factor NICE considers.

teach.body: Know what is in force now. The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions are not yet in force, so the 1983 Act as amended still applies. DoLS remain the live scheme; Liberty Protection Safeguards are not in force. Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026 replaced the 2023 edition, and a new duty to share information about children (Children Act 2004 s16LA) started on 30 September 2026. The National Guardian's Office closed on 30 June 2026.
teach.cite: Mental Health Act 2025; Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026; Children Act 2004 s16LA

teach.caption: Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs (including political views) to people in an inappropriate way. Code 5: keep confidentiality.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Specialist Lena reads an appraisal
teach.body: A new drug costs £30,000 more per person than current care and adds 1.5 QALYs. Lena works out the ICER: £30,000 ÷ 1.5 = £20,000 per QALY gained. That is below NICE's standard range of £25,000–£35,000, so on cost-effectiveness grounds it would usually be considered good value. A drug adding only 0.5 QALYs for the same cost would be £60,000 per QALY, well above the range.

teach.text: Old textbooks quote £20,000–£30,000 per QALY. From 2026 NICE's standard technology appraisal threshold is £25,000–£35,000 per QALY gained.

items: Health is devolved: CQC (England), HIW (Wales), HIS (Scotland), RQIA (Northern Ireland).
Opportunity cost: the health benefit lost from the next best use of the money.
1 QALY = 1 year in perfect health; ICER = extra cost ÷ extra QALYs.
NICE standard threshold: £25,000–£35,000 per QALY gained (2026).
Know what is in force (MHA 1983 as amended, DoLS); influence policy with evidence through proper routes.

summary: You can now describe key devolved differences in UK health systems, explain opportunity cost and QALYs, calculate a cost per QALY and compare it with NICE's 2026 threshold. You can also tell current from coming policy and influence policy in a professional way.

A.q: What does one quality-adjusted life year (QALY) represent?
options: One year of life in any state of health
One year of life in perfect health
One year of life free from hospital care
One year of life gained per £1,000 spent
A.why: NICE: a QALY adjusts length of life for its quality; one QALY equals one year of life in perfect health, with each year weighted by a quality-of-life score from 0 to 1.

whyNot.0: Years in poorer health are weighted below 1, so they count as less than a QALY.
whyNot.2: Hospital use is not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: A QALY measures health, not health per pound spent.

A.q: What is NICE's standard cost-effectiveness threshold for technology appraisals following the 2026 change?
options: £20,000 to £30,000 per QALY gained
£30,000 to £50,000 per QALY gained
£10,000 to £20,000 per QALY gained
£25,000 to £35,000 per QALY gained
A.why: Following a government decision, NICE's standard threshold for technology appraisals rose from £20,000–£30,000 to £25,000–£35,000 per QALY gained (NICE, 2026).

whyNot.0: This was the previous threshold range.
whyNot.1: This range is higher than NICE's standard threshold.
whyNot.2: This range is lower than NICE's standard threshold.

A.q: Which body inspects and regulates healthcare in Wales?
options: Healthcare Inspectorate Wales
The Care Quality Commission
Healthcare Improvement Scotland
The Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority
A.why: Health is devolved. Healthcare Inspectorate Wales regulates healthcare in Wales; the CQC covers England, Healthcare Improvement Scotland covers Scotland and the RQIA covers Northern Ireland.

whyNot.1: The CQC regulates health and social care in England.
whyNot.2: Healthcare Improvement Scotland works in Scotland.
whyNot.3: The RQIA works in Northern Ireland.

B.q: A new treatment costs £12,000 more than current care and gives 0.4 extra QALYs. What is its cost per QALY gained, and how does it compare with NICE's standard range?
options: £4,800 per QALY, well below the range
£48,000 per QALY, above the range
£30,000 per QALY, within the range
£3,000 per QALY, well below the range
B.why: ICER = extra cost ÷ extra QALYs = £12,000 ÷ 0.4 = £30,000 per QALY gained, which lies within NICE's standard range of £25,000–£35,000 (2026).

whyNot.0: This multiplies £12,000 by 0.4 instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: This divides by 4 instead of 0.4; the ICER is £30,000.

B.q: A trust spends its remaining budget on a new scanner, so a planned falls service cannot start. What is the health benefit lost from the falls service called?
options: The incremental cost
The marginal benefit
The QALY threshold
The opportunity cost
B.why: NICE defines opportunity cost as the value of benefits from other healthcare programmes displaced by an intervention, best measured by the health that the next best alternative would have achieved.

whyNot.0: Incremental cost is the extra cost of one option compared with another.
whyNot.1: Marginal benefit is the extra benefit of one more unit of an intervention.
whyNot.2: The QALY threshold is the value NICE uses to judge cost-effectiveness.

B.q: Kemi, a nursing associate registered with the NMC in England, plans to move to Edinburgh. Can she practise there as a nursing associate?
options: Yes, NMC registration covers the whole UK
Yes, after a short Scottish conversion course first
No, nursing associates are regulated in England
No, until she has two years' experience
B.why: The NMC regulates nurses and midwives across the UK, but nursing associates are regulated in England only, an example of devolved differences in workforce policy (P7.2).

whyNot.0: UK-wide registration applies to nurses and midwives, not nursing associates.
whyNot.1: There is no conversion course that extends the role to Scotland.
whyNot.3: Experience does not change where the role is regulated.

C.q: Current care gives 4 years at a quality-of-life score of 0.5. A new treatment gives 4 years at 0.75 and costs £40,000 more. What is the cost per QALY gained?
options: £40,000, above the range
£10,000, below the range
£13,333, below the range
£20,000, below the range
C.why: Current: 4 × 0.5 = 2 QALYs. New: 4 × 0.75 = 3 QALYs. Gain = 1 QALY. ICER = £40,000 ÷ 1 = £40,000 per QALY, above NICE's £25,000–£35,000 range. Two steps: calculate QALYs, then the ratio.

whyNot.1: This divides £40,000 by 4 years without weighting for quality of life.
whyNot.2: This divides by the new treatment's 3 QALYs instead of the 1 QALY gained.
whyNot.3: This divides by the current 2 QALYs instead of the 1 QALY gained.

C.q: In October 2026, a patient's relative says the Mental Health Act 2025 has already replaced section 3 of the 1983 Act. What is the most accurate reply?
options: Yes, the 2025 Act is fully in force
It passed, but most provisions are not yet in force
No, the 2025 Act was withdrawn before Royal Assent
Yes, it is in force in Wales and Northern Ireland first
C.why: The Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 18 December 2025, but most provisions, including changes to sections 3 and 4, were not in force at October 2026; the 1983 Act as amended still applies (P7.4).

whyNot.0: Most provisions had not been brought into force at October 2026.
whyNot.2: The Act did receive Royal Assent, on 18 December 2025.
whyNot.3: The Act has not been brought into force in those nations first.

C.q: Sam, a ward nurse, is concerned that a proposed closure of a local respite unit will increase emergency admissions. Which action best uses political awareness professionally?
options: Ask his patients to sign a petition during care
Post patients' stories on his public social media
Tell patients which party to support at the next election
Submit anonymised admissions data to the consultation
C.why: P7.13 and P5.12 ask nurses to use political awareness and mechanisms for influencing policy. Evidence-based submissions, directly or via professional bodies and unions, are legitimate; Code 5 and 20.7 protect confidentiality and prevent inappropriate expression of political views.

whyNot.0: Lobbying patients during care is an inappropriate use of the professional relationship (Code 20.7).
whyNot.1: Sharing patients' stories publicly breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.2: Expressing political views to patients breaches Code 20.7.

reteach.title: A fixed pot of money
reteach.question: If a family has £100 for the week, how does it decide what to buy?

blocks.body: The NHS, like a family budget, cannot buy everything. A QALY lets very different treatments be compared on the same scale: years of life, weighted by how good those years are. Dividing the extra cost by the extra QALYs gives the cost per QALY. If it is within NICE's range, the treatment is usually good value; if much higher, the money might do more good elsewhere: that lost good is the opportunity cost.

blocks.text: Divide cost by QALYs gained, not by years and not by total QALYs: use the DIFFERENCE between the options.

explain.body: Each UK nation runs its own health system. Regulators: CQC (England), HIW (Wales), HIS (Scotland), RQIA (Northern Ireland). Nursing associates are regulated in England only.

test.q: Which body regulates health and social care services in England?
options: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
Healthcare Improvement Scotland
The National Data Guardian
test.why: The Care Quality Commission is the independent regulator of health and social care services in England.

whyNot.1: The NMC regulates individual nurses, midwives and nursing associates, not services.
whyNot.2: Healthcare Improvement Scotland works in Scotland.
whyNot.3: The National Data Guardian advises on the use of health data.

explain.body: QALYs weight each year of life by a quality-of-life score from 0 (dead) to 1 (perfect health). Years × score = QALYs.

test.q: How many QALYs are produced by 6 years of life at a quality-of-life score of 0.5?
test.why: QALYs = years × quality score = 6 × 0.5 = 3 QALYs (NICE glossary).

whyNot.0: This divides 6 by 5 rather than multiplying by 0.5.
whyNot.2: Six would be correct only at full health (score 1).
whyNot.3: This divides by 0.5 instead of multiplying.

explain.body: ICER = difference in cost ÷ difference in QALYs. Compare with NICE's standard range of £25,000–£35,000 per QALY gained (2026).

test.q: A treatment costs £50,000 more and gives 2 extra QALYs. What is the cost per QALY gained?
test.why: £50,000 ÷ 2 = £25,000 per QALY gained, at the lower end of NICE's 2026 standard range.

explain.body: Use evidence through consultations, elected representatives, professional bodies and unions. Keep information anonymised (Code 5) and do not express political views to people in your care (Code 20.7).

test.q: Which is the most appropriate way for a nurse to influence a proposed health policy change?
options: Responding to the consultation with evidence
Discussing it with patients during care
Sharing patient records with a local journalist
Refusing to work in the new service
test.why: Responding to consultations with evidence is a legitimate mechanism for influencing public policy (P5.12, P7.13).

whyNot.1: Raising political issues with patients during care risks breaching Code 20.7.
whyNot.3: Refusing to work does not influence policy professionally and may harm patients.
